extracted.intended_audience: high-school olympiad students, coaches, and readers of advanced geometry problem collections
extracted.subtask_description: Solution techniques and geometric principles for olympiad-style plane geometry problems (cyclic quadrilaterals, power of a point, dissections, regular polygons). The page collects lemmas, constructions, and recurring methods used to prove contest geometry results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize cyclic quadrilaterals via opposite angles
rubrics_metrics.description: A quadrilateral is cyclic if a pair of opposite angles add up to 180° (or equivalently subtend the same arc).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use angle sums to show two opposite angles are supplementary (examples: ABIC cyclic because BIC + BAC = 180°). Often shown by computing individual angles (angle chasing) or showing equal inscribed angles subtend the same arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bisector and incenter/excenter orthogonality
rubrics_metrics.description: The interior and exterior bisectors of the same angle are orthogonal; incenter I and excenter Ic with C are collinear, and A,B,I,Ic lie on the circle with diameter IIc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit orthogonality to show cyclicity (two opposite right angles) and deduce midpoints/centers: the circumcircle of triangle ABI has center the midpoint of IIc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct rectangles/auxiliary points to create cyclic figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce auxiliary rectangles and points (e.g., choose P so ADMP is a rectangle; choose Q,R so QBDA and ADCR are rectangles) to force cyclic quadrilaterals and parallelism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such constructions can produce circles of given diameters and lead to cyclic quadrilaterals (ADEQ, ADFR), parallel sides (EQ ∥ RF), trapezoids, and useful midpoints (P midpoint of QR) that yield further cyclic quadrilaterals (ADNP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Homothety / common center of homothety reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: If triangles have pairwise parallel sides then either corresponding lines are parallel or they meet at a common center of homothety; use this to locate concurrency and tangency points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical use: show lines DF and EG pass through the intersection Q of CP with circumcircle by proving corresponding angles/subtended arcs and using cyclicity to transfer equal angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of a point (product of segments on a chord)
rubrics_metrics.description: For chords through P on a circle, if AP = a, BP = b, CP = c, DP = d, EP = e, FP = f then ab = cd = ef; use equal chord lengths to deduce set-equalities {a,b} = {c,d} = {e,f}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply to show a point is the center (when chord products/equalities force coinciding circles), to deduce equal products like AE·AF = AB^2, and to prove cyclicity or equality of lengths. Many problems compute powers with respect to several circles and equate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: AM–GM to minimize sum given product in geometric construction
rubrics_metrics.description: When power of a point yields a fixed product xy = ab, minimize x+y via AM–GM; the minimum is attained at x = y = sqrt(ab).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to argue existence of minimal radius or extremal configuration; tie equality case to symmetric placement of points (e.g., M and N chosen so MP = NP = sqrt(ab)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reflections of orthocenter and equal power relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflections of the orthocenter across sides lie on the circumcircle, giving equal products AH·A' H = DH·D' H = EH·E' H, and equal powers relative to circles with given diameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these equalities to show a point has the same power to multiple circles, proving coaxiality of circles or that circles share a common radical axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical axes and radical center concurrency
rubrics_metrics.description: The three radical axes of three circles are either parallel or concur at the radical center; use this to deduce collinearity/concurrency of constructed points (intersections of certain lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical application: show points with equal powers lie on radical axes and therefore conclude collinearity (examples throughout the Power of a Point section).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive similarity from equal chord products to conclude cyclicity
rubrics_metrics.description: If AE·AF = AD·AC then triangles ADE and AFC are similar (sharing angle at A), so DEFC is cyclic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute segment products using given equalities (or power of a point) to recognize similar triangles and thereby deduce cyclic quadrilaterals and subsequent metric conclusions (midpoints, ratios).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use feet of altitudes / orthocenter relations to identify intersection points
rubrics_metrics.description: Feet of altitudes lie on circles of diameters and comparing powers relative to such circles can force intersection coincidences (e.g., X = Y when HX·HP equals other equal products).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct altitudes, locate their feet on relevant circles, compute powers of H to multiple circles, and equate to deduce equality of distances and hence point coincidences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed angles modulo 180° as an angle-chasing tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with directed angles modulo 180° to simplify cyclicity and incidence proofs, especially when dealing with supplementary angles and multiple cyclic quadrilaterals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equality relations like ∠AHF = ∠ADF (mod180°) and combine cyclic quadrilateral facts to locate circumcenters and radical axes; helps avoid sign/orientation pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent-chord angle and homothety to map tangents
rubrics_metrics.description: The angle between a chord and tangent equals the inscribed angle subtending the chord; homotheties map tangency points and can be used to show an image line is tangent to a target circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., map a circle by homothety to relate tangents: an angle at D equals the tangent angle to ω3 and maps to a tangent to ω2, proving line PQ is tangent to both ω1 and ω2 and identifying common tangency points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Pascal's theorem to deduce collinearity in degenerate cyclic hexagons
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Pascal to a (possibly degenerate) cyclic hexagon formed by tangents and points to deduce collinearity of intersection points of opposite sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: degenerate cyclic hexagon ABBRCC gives collinear points N, D, M and shows BN and CM meet on circumcircle; useful for angle conclusions like showing BN and CM form 60°.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce auxiliary points and continuity/perturbation arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose auxiliary points close to sides or positions so that some continuous quantity varies; by continuity one obtains the desired configuration where an angle sum equals 180° or cyclicity holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in dissection/constructive problems: pick P close to AD to guarantee existence of Q on AD with ARPQ cyclic via continuity; similarly used to generate trapezoid/cyclic decompositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rotation by special angles (hidden rotation trick)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify a rotation (often 60° for equilateral triangle problems, 45° for squares) that maps one segment/point to another; this can reveal equilateral triangles or locate centers via rotation+dilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., obtain equilateral triangle AQN by showing AQ = AN and ∠QAN = 60°, or produce a center of a square by 45° rotation followed by contraction by 1/√2. This is often a constructive insight in olympiad problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex numbers for rotations and dilations
rubrics_metrics.description: Model rotations and contractions using complex numbers to express transforms succinctly and carry algebraic proofs of geometric constructions (useful for centers and symmetry operations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when rotations/dilations combine; offers an algebraic alternative to pure synthetic rotation+ratio arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissection by induction (squares/cubes into many smaller copies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove existence of dissections for all sufficiently large n by base constructions and an induction step that increases the number of pieces (e.g., divide one square into 4 to increase count by 3; divide a cube into 8 to increase by 7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit base decompositions for small n (6,7,8 or 55–61 for cubes) then iterate the operation to get all larger n by adding fixed increments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edge-counting and parity arguments to show impossibility in dissections
rubrics_metrics.description: Count edges/vertices or use parity/tiling-coloring arguments to show certain dissections cannot exist (e.g., square cannot be partitioned into 5 smaller squares).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how many smaller squares touch sides, possible L-shaped remainders, and derive contradictions from side-length equalities or combinatorial counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize polygons dissectable into parallelograms via center of symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: A convex polygon can be dissected into parallelograms iff it has a center of symmetry (opposite sides parallel and congruent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof direction: dissectability implies paired parallel congruent sides; conversely, use induction removing suitable parallelograms to build dissection for any centrally symmetric polygon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear Diophantine constraints for rectangle-similarity dissections
rubrics_metrics.description: When dissecting a rectangle into n similar rectangles, side-length ratios satisfy linear relations with integer coefficients; determinant conditions (from system of linear equations) control feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set A = n1 a + n2 b, B = n3 a + n4 b for small-rectangle sides a,b and deduce determinant constraints; irrationality of √n may force trivial decompositions (all small rectangles aligned).

rubrics_metrics.name: Area-sum via orthogonal path intersections
rubrics_metrics.description: In rectangular dissections where neighboring rectangles share full sides, represent families of rectangles as crossroads of orthogonal path families; the sum of areas of rectangles equals the number of such families (gives total area n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct L1 and L2 segments on orthogonal sides; each path-pair intersection corresponds to exactly one rectangle of area L1L2; summing over families yields the total area equals n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of similarity and arc-angle relations to deduce concurrency/collinearity
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate equal angles obtained via similarity and arc-subtending relations to prove lines are parallel or intersect at a common point; often used to conclude collinearity of constructed points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: showing P1B1 ∥ A2P2 and other parallelisms to prove perspective triangles and hence collinearity (Pascal/Pappus-style configurations).
